title: What ChatGPT Thinks It Knows About You Is Affecting Its Answers. Here’s How to Change That
gist: ChatGPT's memory feature, launched in April 2024 requiring explicit 'remember this' commands, was reworked in June into an automatic system OpenAI calls dreaming, where memories are built and edited over time without user requests — which personalizes answers but hands the model, not the user, control over what it believes about you.

themes.theme: From explicit recall to automatic profiling

insights.claim: When ChatGPT's memory feature launched in April 2024, users had to explicitly say 'remember this' or the detail was lost, and stored memories were fixed — a mentioned upcoming party would still be treated as future even after the date passed.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Establishes how recently persistent AI memory was primitive; the state of the art is moving on a sub-two-year cadence.
insights.locator: When ChatGPT first introduced a memory feature back in April 2024

insights.claim: After a June update, ChatGPT performs what OpenAI calls dreaming: memories are flexible, built up and edited over time, and saved and sifted automatically so manual requests are no longer needed.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Automatic persistent user models are the new competitive surface for consumer AI — the switching-cost moat chatbots previously lacked.
insights.quote: Memories are now flexible, and are now built up and edited over time—so ChatGPT knows the party is in the past, not the future.
insights.locator: After an update in June, ChatGPT now does something called dreaming

insights.claim: OpenAI states the three aims of memory are to carry forward useful context, follow preferences and constraints, and stay current over time.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Vendor-stated design goals reveal the product direction: an always-on user model rather than session-scoped assistance.
insights.locator: OpenAI says the three main aims of memory

insights.claim: Because the chatbot rather than the user now decides what is important enough to remember, it continually refines assumptions about the user and will not always assess them correctly — a week researching a light switch can leave it convinced you are a DIY enthusiast.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Silent personalization drift means AI outputs are no longer reproducible across users, complicating any workflow that assumes consistent model behavior.
insights.quote: Essentially, it's now down to the chatbot rather than you to decide what's important enough to be remembered
insights.locator: Essentially, it's now down to the chatbot

insights.claim: Every response now carries memory context, so accumulated inferences change answers in ways the user did not ask for and may not want.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Enterprise and research users relying on chatbot outputs need memory hygiene or temporary chats to avoid contaminated results.
insights.quote: All the bot's answers come with memory context now.
insights.locator: Perhaps you've spent a week researching how to replace a light switch

insights.claim: Users get less control over automatic memory than they might expect, even though the stated goal is helpfully tuned personalization.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: The gap between stated user control and actual control is the regulatory attack surface for AI personalization.
insights.quote: Ideally, that should mean responses that are tuned and personalized in helpful ways, but you don't get as much control over this as you might expect.
insights.locator: OpenAI says the three main aims of memory

insights.claim: Turning off ChatGPT's memory toggle stops new remembering and stops the model referring to existing memories, but the stored memories are retained in case the user re-enables the feature.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Disabling a privacy feature is not deletion — a distinction that matters for data-retention compliance claims.
insights.quote: You can turn this off to stop ChatGPT from remembering anything you say, but this won't wipe out existing memories
insights.locator: The first thing you'll see is a toggle switch

insights.claim: Even after deleting memory entirely, past conversations remain, and turning memory back on causes those chats to be indexed all over again as the model rebuilds its profile of the user.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Profile deletion is reversible by design, meaning user erasure requests against chat history are the binding control, not the memory switch.
insights.quote: your past conversations don't go anywhere, and if you turn memory back on, these chats will be indexed all over again as ChatGPT tries to figure out who you are
insights.locator: To wipe everything, select the three dots at the top

insights.claim: ChatGPT exposes memory as an editable summary where users can highlight entries and choose 'Make a correction' or 'Don't mention this again', or issue prompt-box commands such as forgetting a stated profession.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Granular memory editing is becoming table stakes for consumer AI UX; absence of it is a differentiator rivals can attack.
insights.locator: Choose Manage next to Memory summaries

insights.claim: Temporary chats commit nothing to memory and are forgotten as soon as they are closed, providing the only clean-room mode inside the product.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: A deliberate no-memory mode is the practical workaround for sensitive or benchmark-style queries.
insights.locator: There's also a temporary chat feature available
